questions.stem: During design development, the client asks the architect to study two additional site layouts not included in the agreed scope. What should the architect do first?

options.text: Prepare the layouts to maintain goodwill, then bill for them at the end of the phase.
options.explanation: Doing work first and billing later invites disputes. The client never agreed to pay.

options.text: Notify the client in writing that this is an additional service, state the fee and schedule impact, and get written authorization before proceeding.
options.explanation: Correct. Prompt written notice and authorization prevent scope creep and payment disputes.

options.text: Refuse, since the work isn't in the contract.
options.explanation: The architect can provide additional services. Refusing outright is unnecessary and harms the relationship.

options.text: Absorb the cost but reduce construction administration hours later to compensate.
options.explanation: Secretly cutting other services to recover fee risks breaching the agreement and the standard of care.

questions.explanation: Scope creep control: recognize → notify in writing → state the impact → get authorization → then proceed.

questions.stem: A client's maximum design fee is 15% below the architect's proposal for full services. Which negotiation strategy is most appropriate?

options.text: Accept the lower fee and keep the full scope to win the project.
options.explanation: Discounting without changing scope puts the project's profitability, and possibly its quality, at risk.

options.text: Adjust the scope to match the fee, for example by moving construction administration to hourly or removing renderings.
options.explanation: Correct. Trading scope for fee keeps the fee aligned with the services provided.

options.text: Accept the fee and plan to make up the difference through additional services.
options.explanation: Planning to recover fee through change requests is poor faith dealing and damages trust.

options.text: Lower the standard of care in the agreement.
options.explanation: The standard of care can't be bargained down to save fee.

questions.explanation: Negotiate scope and fee together. If the fee moves, the scope moves.

questions.stem: A contractor asks for the architect's native BIM model to help prepare shop drawings. Which measures protect the architect?

options.text: Releasing the model under a digital data license that limits use to this project
options.explanation: Correct. A license (e.g., AIA C106) defines permitted use and protects the architect's IP.

options.text: Stating that the model isn't a contract document and that the contractor is responsible for verifying dimensions
options.explanation: Correct. A reliance disclaimer keeps the sealed contract documents controlling and puts the duty to verify on the contractor.

options.text: Transferring the model's copyright to the contractor
options.explanation: There's no reason to give up ownership. A license is enough.

options.text: Releasing the model with no agreement to save time
options.explanation: Releasing files without terms invites misuse and reliance claims.

options.text: Agreeing that shop drawings made from the model need no architect review
options.explanation: The architect still reviews submittals under the contract documents.

options.text: Warranting that the model is free of errors
options.explanation: A warranty creates uninsurable exposure and contradicts the reliance disclaimer.

questions.explanation: Digital files: license the use, disclaim reliance, keep ownership.

questions.stem: Which fee method is most appropriate for a renovation feasibility study where the existing conditions and the scope are very uncertain?

options.text: Stipulated sum
options.explanation: A fixed fee for an unclear scope puts the architect at risk of significant overruns.

options.text: Hourly, possibly with a not-to-exceed amount agreed with the client
options.explanation: Correct. Hourly billing matches fee to effort when the scope is uncertain. A cap gives the client some cost control.

options.text: Percentage of construction cost
options.explanation: There's no reliable construction cost yet for a feasibility study.

options.text: Unit cost per square foot
options.explanation: Unit pricing suits repetitive, predictable work, not uncertain studies.

questions.stem: Midway through construction documents, the owner doubles the project's size. Under B101-2017, what generally applies?

options.text: The architect must absorb the change, since the fee is a stipulated sum.
options.explanation: A material change in project scope calls for an equitable adjustment, even under a stipulated sum.

options.text: The architect's compensation and schedule should be equitably adjusted for the material change in scope.
options.explanation: Correct. B101-2017 provides for adjusting compensation when the project's or the services' scope changes materially.

options.text: The agreement terminates automatically.
options.explanation: The agreement continues. The change is handled by adjusting compensation and schedule.

options.text: The contractor pays the additional design fee.
options.explanation: The design fee is owed by the owner under the owner–architect agreement.

questions.explanation: Material scope change → equitable adjustment of fee and schedule.

questions.stem: An owner terminates the B101-2017 agreement for convenience after construction documents are complete and wants to use the documents to build the project with another architect. What does B101-2017 provide?

options.text: The owner automatically owns the documents upon termination.
options.explanation: The architect keeps the copyright. The owner holds a license whose terms depend on the circumstances of termination.

options.text: The owner may use the documents if it pays the licensing fee set in the agreement and other amounts owed, and it releases the architect from liability for their use.
options.explanation: Correct. Under B101-2017, continued use after termination for convenience is conditioned on the licensing fee. Use without the architect is at the owner's risk.

options.text: The owner may never use the documents after termination.
options.explanation: The agreement provides a path, via the licensing fee, for the owner to keep using them.

options.text: The new architect becomes the copyright owner by sealing the documents.
options.explanation: Sealing someone else's documents doesn't transfer copyright, and it raises responsible-control issues.

questions.explanation: Copyright stays with the architect; the license is conditioned on payment; a licensing fee applies after termination for convenience.
questions.confidenceNote: Summarizes B101-2017 Article 7 / §11.9 as I understand them. Confirm the exact conditions in your copy.

questions.stem: Which practices help a firm control scope creep across its projects?

options.text: Defining scope, deliverables and assumptions clearly in the agreement
options.explanation: Correct. A clear baseline makes changes recognizable.

options.text: Training project managers to identify out-of-scope requests and route them through a change process
options.explanation: Correct. Most scope creep happens at the project-team level.

options.text: Setting basic-service limits, such as the number of site visits and submittal reviews
options.explanation: Correct. Quantified limits make additional services objective.

options.text: Agreeing to 'unlimited revisions' in the proposal
options.explanation: Unlimited revisions invite unbounded scope.

options.text: Avoiding written meeting minutes so the client feels less constrained
options.explanation: Documentation is how changes are recognized and authorized.

options.text: Providing minor extra services without comment to build goodwill
options.explanation: Unacknowledged favors set expectations and add up to real scope creep.

questions.explanation: Define the baseline, set limits, train teams, and document.

questions.stem: Which fee method most clearly creates an appearance of conflict of interest about project cost?

options.text: Percentage of construction cost
options.explanation: Correct. The architect's fee rises as construction cost rises, which can appear to reward more expensive design.

options.text: Stipulated sum
options.explanation: A fixed fee doesn't change with construction cost.

options.text: Hourly with a not-to-exceed amount
options.explanation: Hourly fees track effort, not construction cost.

options.text: Unit cost per apartment unit
options.explanation: Per-unit fees track unit count, not cost.

questions.explanation: Percentage-of-cost fees are simple, but they tie compensation to construction cost.

questions.stem: A firm has developed a proprietary curtain-wall detail library that gives it a competitive edge. Which protection is most appropriate for keeping it confidential?

options.text: Treat it as a trade secret, with access controls and confidentiality agreements for staff and consultants.
options.explanation: Correct. Trade-secret protection depends on reasonable measures to keep the information confidential.

options.text: Publish it to establish copyright.
options.explanation: Publishing destroys confidentiality, and copyright exists without publication.

options.text: Register it as a trademark.
options.explanation: Trademarks protect brand identifiers such as names and logos, not technical details.

options.text: Rely on the AIA Code of Ethics to stop departing employees from using it.
options.explanation: The Code guides members but isn't a substitute for contractual and security protections.

questions.explanation: Match the IP tool to the asset: copyright for expression, trademark for brand, trade secret for confidential know-how.

questions.stem: During negotiations, an owner wants to cut the architect's construction-phase services entirely to save fee. What is the architect's most appropriate response?

options.text: Agree, since the owner controls the scope.
options.explanation: The owner decides, but the architect should first explain the risks so the decision is informed.

options.text: Explain the risks of losing construction-phase services (submittal review, RFIs, observation, payment certification) and offer alternatives such as a limited or hourly CA scope.
options.explanation: Correct. Informing the owner of the consequences and offering scaled options protects the project and clarifies responsibility.

options.text: Agree, and offer to answer contractor questions for free.
options.explanation: Informal free services create liability without the protections of a defined scope.

options.text: Refuse to sign any agreement without full CA.
options.explanation: Refusing outright may be unnecessary. A limited, defined scope can be appropriate if the risks are understood and documented.

questions.explanation: When scope is cut, explain the consequences, offer alternatives, and document the owner's choice.

flashcards.back: Define scope first. If the fee must drop, reduce or restructure scope; don't just discount.
Gradual, unacknowledged growth of services beyond the agreed scope.

flashcards.front: How to handle an out-of-scope request
flashcards.back: Notify in writing → state the fee and schedule impact → get written authorization → then proceed.
Agreed numbers of submittal reviews, site visits, and inspections for substantial and final completion. Beyond them is an additional service.
Equitable adjustment of compensation and schedule (B101-2017 §11.6).

flashcards.front: Best fee type for uncertain scope
flashcards.back: Hourly (time-based), optionally with a not-to-exceed cap.
The architect absorbs overruns, so it's best when scope is well defined.
The fee rises with cost (appearance of conflict) and falls when cost is cut.

flashcards.front: Owner's rights in instruments of service (B101-2017)
flashcards.back: A nonexclusive license for the project, conditioned on meeting obligations including payment. The architect keeps copyright.
Payable for continued use of the documents if the owner terminates for convenience (§11.9).
BIM and Digital Data Exhibit. Sets protocols for digital data and BIM (used with G201/G202).
Digital Data Licensing Agreement, for sharing files with a party you have no other contract with.
Confidential business know-how, protected by keeping it secret (access controls, NDAs).
Stipulated sum for design phases + hourly for construction administration and additional services.
